title: Synapse analysis declaration
description: THE DEMAND SIDE. What a consumer NEEDS, as data. The capability and signal contracts describe what Synapse OFFERS; nothing described what anything REQUIRED, so an analysis's inputs could only be discovered by running it. EXTRACTED from writing dead_stock, not designed in advance: every field here exists because that declaration could not be written without it, and the two fields most likely to be wanted next (a schedule, and an output destination) are still ABSENT: an evaluator now consumes a declaration and produces rows, but nothing SCHEDULES one or DELIVERS the result anywhere, so both fields would still be guesses about shapes no caller has asked for.

version.description: SemVer, matching the capability contract's discipline. A rule whose threshold or inputs change is a different rule, and a consumer must be able to pin which one it ran.

grain.description: The columns that together identify ONE emitted row. MUST BE CONTAINED IN EVERY REQUIRED CAPABILITY'S GRAIN, checked at registry import — an analysis emitting one row per (tenant, store, sku) can only join capabilities that identify rows at least that finely, and a coarser capability cannot be joined without inventing rows. This is the first mechanical use of the capability contract's `grain`, and the reason that field was worth extracting from one resolver.

requires.description: The capabilities this analysis reads, with the fields it reads from each and the gates it binds on each. NON-EMPTY: an analysis with no inputs has nothing to analyse.

capability_id.description: Must name a REGISTERED capability. A requirement on an unregistered one is a declaration that can never resolve; a requirement on a DECLINED one fails at import with the recorded reason attached.

fields.description: The subset of that capability's `returns` this analysis reads. Checked against `returns` at import, which is what would catch reaching for a plausible-but-absent field — the most likely way an analysis goes quietly wrong. NON-EMPTY: an analysis that reads nothing from a capability does not require it.

gates.description: Thresholds this analysis binds on that capability's declared gate KINDS, each with the policy for reducing a per-series measurement to a verdict. THIS IS THE FIELD THE CAPABILITY CONTRACT GAVE UP: it held `min_history_days: 60` on the supply side, which works for one caller and breaks for two — dead stock wants 90 days of no-sales, a forecast wants 60 for seasonality, and both read the same rows. An EMPTY ARRAY is a claim that the capability declares no gates, and the binding must match its declared kinds exactly: an unbound declared gate never runs, and a bound undeclared gate has no probe.

days.description: Minimum DISTINCT dates carrying data, per series — coverage, not calendar span. A forecaster needs observations, not distance. Minimum 1: zero is not a requirement, it is the absence of one, and the empty array says that.

policy.description: What 'enough' MEANS across a population of series. all_series = every series must clear the threshold ('forecast every SKU'); any_series = one qualifying series is enough ('forecast anything', and what a console asking 'is this usable here at all' means). Both are legitimate and neither is derivable from data, which is why a caller must state it and why slice 1's unowned default was deleted rather than tuned. MIN-over-series is deliberately not a value: it is all_series with a worse name, and it reads as conservative while being unusable on any growing catalogue.

emits.description: The field names this analysis PRODUCES. Declared before anything consumes them on purpose: the day a scorer or an action arrives it is checkable against this rather than against whatever the code happened to return.

thresholds.description: Numbers the ANALYSIS ITSELF uses, as distinct from gates on a capability. A gate decides whether a capability may be READ; a threshold is arithmetic over rows already fetched. dead_stock's stale_after_days is the second kind: no read depends on it, and it is the whole content of the rule.

fitted.description: TRUE when the number is derived from the tenant's own data. FALSE when it is a constant, in which case `stands_in_for` is REQUIRED — a number with no stated derivation is indistinguishable from a number someone guessed, and the standing rule is that thresholds are fitted where possible and honest about it where not.

stands_in_for.description: What a CONSTANT threshold substitutes for, and ideally how the fitted version would be computed. Required when fitted is false, forbidden when it is true (a fitted threshold stands in for nothing).
